title: The hours
hookLine: monks stop work seven times a day to pray: nothing is to be preferred to the work of God

cards: "Seven times a day do I praise thee." That's a line from Psalm 119, and Benedict took it at its word.
In his Rule he builds the monastery's day around it: seven times in the daylight hours, the community stops and goes to chapel to pray.
And from the same psalm, "At midnight I will rise to give thanks unto thee," so there's prayer in the night as well. The bell rings, and whatever's in your hands goes down. The bread half kneaded.
The book open at the page. The row half hoed. Christians call this rhythm the hours, or the Divine Office, still kept in monasteries, and by some people outside them.

teach.b: The hours have old names. Lauds at daybreak, then Prime. Terce, Sext and None, spread through the working day.
Vespers as the light goes. Compline before sleep. Each is short: psalms, a reading, a hymn, a prayer.
The heart of it is the Psalms, sung or said together, and the Rule sets them out so the community prays through the whole psalter every week. Then comes the signal.

In the chapter on what to do when it sounds, Benedict says: as soon as you hear it, leave whatever you have in hand and go, quickly, but with seriousness, not giddy. And then the phrase this day is built on.

teach.h: NOTHING BEFORE THE WORK OF GOD.
teach.b: Nothing, he says, is to be put before the Work of God. That's his name for the hours: the Work of God, opus Dei. Not a break from work.
Work. The hours don't pull the monk away from life. They stitch it together.

Kitchen, field, library, chapel, kitchen again. Prayer is the thread running through the day, pulling it tight at regular points so the day can't unravel into one long blur. The Bible already knew the shape.
A psalm says, "Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray." Daniel, in Babylon, kneels three times a day and gives thanks, even when it's against the law. The monks just set the clock by it.
Anyone can keep a small version: stop, put the thing down, turn toward God, or simply toward the quiet, for a minute, and pick it back up.

how: Monks and nuns pray the hours together in chapel at set times of day and night; some Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran Christians pray a shorter form at home, often morning and evening prayer.

games.q: the shape of the monk's day — tap the pairs.

s: Benedict treats the hours as a break from work
he calls them the Work of God, opus Dei.
the seven times a day comes from a psalm
seven times a day do I praise thee.
at the signal, the Rule says, finish what you're doing first
leave whatever is in hand and go, quickly but seriously.

games.q: you're a monk halfway through kneading bread. the bell rings for prayer. what does the Rule ask?
o: put it down and go now, without rushing like a fool.
pray where you stand and keep kneading.
games.why: leave whatever is in hand and hurry, but with seriousness: nothing is to be put before the Work of God.

practice: Choose three moments that already happen in your day, the first coffee, lunch, the drive home, and set a reminder if that helps. Then try the first one now: put down whatever's in your hands and sit still.
If you pray, say a line of a psalm you know, or simply God's name; if you don't, just stop, and notice the day you're in.

wordCard.voice: The hours. The Divine Office: set times of prayer through the day and night, which Benedict calls the Work of God.

orig.note: Latin, the Rule of Saint Benedict's name for the hours of prayer: the Work of God.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing before prayer. Bread down, bell ringing. Back tomorrow, same hill.
